extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of English literature learning/practising close reading and practical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for reading, construing, and judging lyric and sonnet-form poetry, focusing on sense, form, rhythm, diction, and the reader’s technique. Emphasises close analysis of both matter and manner and avoidance of personal or doctrinal prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the poem’s thought through to the end
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader should follow the thought of the poem through to the end rather than confining judgement to isolated features of treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example praise that confines itself to questions of 'treatment' is insufficient; full comprehension requires tracking the poem’s idea to its conclusion to judge its success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider both treatment (manner) and content (matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not consider treatment or content exclusively — both matter (what is said) and manner (how it is said) must be attended to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To consider either treatment or content alone is a means of keeping at a distance from the actual poem. Balanced comments address imagery, diction, rhythm, and thought together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to construe ordinary English (syntactic parsing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reader must be trained to 'construe' ordinary English sentences in the poem to extract meaning; failure to do so impairs further criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching should include practice in parsing sentences; instances where readers cannot construe lines (e.g., misreading 'his very urn') show practical importance of this skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity/lucidity of sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the meaning is clear on first or subsequent readings and whether obscurity is a defect or an artistic device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscurity can be a flaw (making a poem a 'puzzle' rather than a poem) or an added relish if it entices repeated reading. Note which lines are obscure and whether obscurity serves effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and metre as evidence (but context-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate metre and rhythmic regularity/irregularity and how they contribute to mood, sincerity, or emphasis, while recognizing rhythm is dependent on the whole response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irregular metre can emphasize sincerity or force; but rhythm alone may mislead — it must be tested in fullest contact with thought and diction. Examples: irregular Brooke-like sonnets; accenting choices (e.g., 'will') change sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonnet construction and division (octave/sestet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the technical construction of sonnets, especially the presence and effectiveness of a definite division between octave and sestet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'definite division' is often expected; arbitrary adherence to sonnet-form dogma should be questioned. Note whether the sestet works as a development/turn from the octave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, coherence, and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the poem presents ordered thought and coherence rather than being a collection of flashy phrases or disjointed sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coherence is a central poetic difficulty; incoherence may be a 'stunt'. Readers should look for logical/semantic links and unity of argument or feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity/genuineness of utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the poem expresses conviction or is merely playing with an idea — sincerity often shown by control and depth rather than theatrical passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhythmic signs may suggest sincerity but are not decisive; date/context offer presumptive evidence but final judgment comes from fuller contact with poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Striving after effect / artificial mannerisms (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for conscious striving after startling words, forced phrases, or 'poetic' diction that ring false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'unimpeachable body' as far-fetched; forced rhyme-words (e.g., 'slay' used unsuitably). Such striving suggests facade rather than genuine feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and freshness of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether language is simple and natural or affected and 'poetic' in a way that undermines authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for 'simple yet forcible language' contrasts with criticism of false 'poetic diction' or 'unctuously poetic' phrasing. Freedom and neologism can be virtues (e.g., 'wanwood leafmeal') when they compress meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery and concreteness vs abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether images are vivid, living, and concrete enough to support the thought, or whether abstraction weakens the poem’s emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If description of beauty lacks vividness the tragic emphasis may fail; imagery should make the thought perceptible (e.g., 'moulded image' and 'human body' present in thought).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound-patterns and phonetic devices (alliteration, rhyme, vowel music)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the poem’s use of sound — alliteration, rhyme, internal vowel patterns — as integral to its effect and sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound may sometimes dominate attention, causing readers to attend to word-patterns at expense of sense; but skilful interweaving of sound and sense (e.g., vowel music, rhymes) can be central to communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing, crescendo, and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe how temporal shaping (crescendo, quickening or slowing movement) and restraint of language contribute to intensity and closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a sonnet whose sextet quickens via extra syllables and sibilants culminating in monosyllables; restraint can make a crescendo effective and mark final close.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple readings and sensitivity to alternative accents/intonations
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem may yield different senses under different accentuation or readings; critics should test variant readings (e.g., accenting 'will').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors’ marks (accent-marks) or different stress patterns can produce large rhythmical and interpretive differences; repeated attacks and paraphrase often clarify meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of paraphrase and close analytic notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrase and detailed analysis can uncover alternative meanings and help readers who fail on first reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert paraphrases when many readers struggle; paraphrase shows possible readings (e.g., elderly man explaining Margaret’s grief) and helps reveal ambiguous central lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of form to content (fit of form to theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the chosen form (prayer-like metre, sonnet structure, conversational tone) suits and reinforces the poem’s subject and atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Form fits the contents to perfection' is praise; when form and content clash, critique should note the mismatch rather than praise form alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of reader’s doctrinal or personal prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Critic should not allow personal doctrinal biases or tastes (the 'bee') to determine the poem’s worth; these prejudices can distort judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether one is religious/sceptical or favouring traditional/advanced positions should be set aside when judging poem’s merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional communication and potency
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how fully the poem communicates feeling to the reader — whether emotions like sorrow are conveyed poignantly and universally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of high praise note emotions 'lose nothing in communication' and that last lines 'stick in the throat like real sorrow'; lack of communicated feeling is a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs imitation and period-sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether style is genuinely original or an imitation of other poets; date may indicate likelihood of genuineness but not conclusively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation of a past manner may be hollow; knowing a poem’s date offers presumptive evidence about sincerity but final judgment requires contact with poem itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of stance toward sentimentality (avoid cheap reassurance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify when a poem trades in cheap reassurance or sentimental clichés rather than serious insight; label and explain such 'sentimentality'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track stock resonances and vacuous phrases (e.g., 'its essential self in its own season') and show how they produce hollow effects rather than depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability and technical legibility (scannability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lines are metrically or syntactically awkward to the point of impeding reading, this diminishes the poem’s value unless deliberately justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lines that are hard to scan or read ('Nor mouth had, no, nor mind expressed / What heart heard of, ghost guessed') may repel readers; explain whether difficulty is accidental or purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess intentional flatness or banality as technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish genuine defects from intentionally ugly/flat/banal lines used for specific effect; judge their intentionality and success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a final line is 'ugly and flat and banal' but plausibly intentional, interpret as a rhetorical device and evaluate if it serves the poem's aim.
